claim: Zebrafish tenocytes express two Scx orthologues, scxa and scxb.
source: Tenocytes in zebrafish express two Scx orthologues, scxa and scxb (Chen and Galloway, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen and Galloway, 2014

claim: Expression of scxa:mCherry was first detected at 20 hpf in muscle and tendon progenitors of the somites.
source: Expression of scxa:mCherry was first detected at 20 hpf in muscle and tendon progenitors of the somites.
evidence: Observation from transgenic zebrafish line Tg(scxa:mCherry)

claim: By 24 hpf, scxa:mCherry expression in muscle progenitors diminished and became progressively restricted to scattered tendon progenitors along the HMS and VMS (~24 cells per VMS).
source: By 24 hpf, as the first myofibers differentiated, scxa:mCherry expression in muscle progenitors diminished and became progressively restricted to scattered tendon progenitors along the HMS and VMS (~24 cells per VMS) (Figure 1A,D,G) (Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: Quantitative observation from live imaging and figure data

claim: Cells with the highest levels of scxa:mCherry expression were located laterally, adjacent to the HMS, while more medial cells expressed lower levels.
source: Cells with the highest levels of scxa:mCherry expression were located laterally, adjacent to the HMS, while more medial cells expressed lower levels (Figure 1A', D', G').
evidence: Observation from confocal imaging showing spatial expression patterns

claim: By 36 hpf, scxa:mCherry+ cells doubled in number (~44/VMS) and became increasingly localized to the HMS and VMS at future MTJs.
source: By 36 hpf, scxa:mCherry+ cells doubled in number (~44/VMS) and became increasingly localized to the HMS and VMS at future MTJs (Figure 1B,E,H) (Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: Quantitative cell counting from imaging data

claim: At 36 hpf, cells with the highest scxa:mCherry expression that were located medially and in the ventral somites began to extend projections laterally along the VMS, perpendicular to the orientation of muscle fibers.
source: At this stage, cells with the highest scxa:mCherry expression that were located medially and in the ventral somites began to extend projections laterally along the VMS, perpendicular to the orientation of muscle fibers (Figure 1B', E', H').
evidence: Morphological observation from confocal imaging

claim: By 48 hpf tenocyte projections extended 70–80 μm.
source: By 48 hpf these projections extended 70–80 μm (Figure 1C,F,I).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from imaging data

claim: 3D-reconstructions of confocal stacks at 60 hpf revealed that the polarized network of tenocyte projections covered the entire VMS.
source: 3D-reconstructions of confocal stacks at 60 hpf revealed that this polarized network of tenocyte projections covered the entire VMS (Figure 1C', F', I'; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: 3D reconstruction analysis from confocal microscopy

claim: Time-lapsed videos of Tg(scxa:mCherry) embryos capturing images at 20 min intervals from 48 to 60 hpf showed that tenocyte projections are dynamic and constantly changing in length and branching pattern.
source: Time-lapsed videos of Tg(scxa:mCherry) embryos capturing images at 20 min intervals from 48 to 60 hpf showed that tenocyte projections are dynamic and constantly changing in length and branching pattern (Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging data showing temporal dynamics

claim: Tenocytes along the HMS near the NC have shorter, more convoluted projections than tenocytes along the VMS.
source: Tenocytes along the HMS near the NC have shorter, more convoluted projections than tenocytes along the VMS (Figure 1I'; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Comparative morphological observation from imaging

claim: During the period in which axial muscles in the trunk begin to contract and embryos become motile, tenocytes align along future MTJs and undergo dramatic changes in cell shape that correlate with the establishment and strengthening of muscle attachments.
source: Thus, during the period in which axial muscles in the trunk begin to contract and embryos become motile, tenocytes align along future MTJs and undergo dramatic changes in cell shape that correlate with the establishment and strengthening of muscle attachments.
evidence: Correlation observed between timing of muscle contraction and tenocyte morphological changes

claim: A cluster of scxa:mCherry+ tenocyte progenitors is first observed at 36 hpf in the ventral midline near the future attachment sites of the sternohyoideus (SH) and adductor mandibulae (AM).
source: A cluster of scxa:mCherry+ tenocyte progenitors is first observed at 36 hpf in the ventral midline near the future attachment sites of the sternohyoideus (SH) and adductor mandibulae (AM), which are among the earliest muscles to differentiate at 53 hpf (Schilling and Kimmel, 1997).
evidence: Observation from transgenic line with citation for muscle differentiation timing

claim: By 48 hpf, three major clusters of scxa:mCherry+ tenocytes are visible ventrally in the head.
source: By 48 hpf, three major clusters of scxa:mCherry+ tenocytes are visible ventrally, one anterior that forms ventral mandibular, hyoid, and oculomotor muscle tendons and two posterior clusters associated with each SH (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Observation from imaging of cranial tenocytes

claim: The anterior cluster of cranial tenocytes subdivides over 14 hr into separate attachment sites for mandibular (IMA, IMP, AM) and hyoid (IH) muscles.
source: The anterior cluster subdivides over 14 hr into separate attachment sites for mandibular (IMA, IMP, AM) and hyoid (IH) muscles (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Temporal observation from time-course imaging

claim: Double labeling with anti-MHC and anti-mCherry antibodies revealed a tight correlation between the timing of the onset of muscle contraction and tenocyte morphogenesis in cranial muscle clusters.
source: Double labeling with anti-MHC and anti-mCherry antibodies revealed a tight correlation between the timing of the onset of muscle contraction and tenocyte morphogenesis in each of these clusters (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B,D,E,G,H).
evidence: Immunostaining data showing temporal correlation

claim: Cranial myofibers remain immotile at 48–62 hpf and their corresponding tenocytes form clusters of rounded cells at future attachment sites.
source: Cranial myofibers remain immotile at 48–62 hpf and their corresponding tenocytes form clusters of rounded cells at future attachment sites.
evidence: Observation of cell morphology during development

claim: Cranial tenocytes undergo compaction and elongation as contractions begin at 72 hpf.
source: These tenocytes then undergo compaction and elongation as contractions begin at 72 hpf (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,F,I).
evidence: Morphological observation correlated with muscle contraction timing

claim: Embryos injected with αBtx mRNA at the one-cell stage were completely paralyzed until 60 hpf, after which they gradually recovered motility as αBtx activity declined.
source: Embryos injected with αBtx mRNA at the one-cell stage were completely paralyzed until 60 hpf, after which they gradually recovered motility as αBtx activity declined.
evidence: Experimental observation of paralysis phenotype

claim: Depth-coded, 3D-reconstructed images of living trunk tenocytes along the MTJs of somites 16–17 at 48 hpf revealed an average reduction of 13 μm (18%) in axial tenocyte projection length in αBtx-injected embryos compared to uninjected controls.
source: Depth-coded, 3D-reconstructed images of living trunk tenocytes along the MTJs of somites 16–17 at 48 hpf revealed an average reduction of 13 μm (18%) in axial tenocyte projection length in αBtx-injected embryos compared to uninjected controls (Figure 2A,B,E).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from 3D imaging analysis

claim: Paralyzed embryos showed reduced branching complexity in their tenocyte projections.
source: Paralyzed embryos also showed reduced branching complexity in their projections (Figure 2F) and projection density along the VMS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of branching patterns from imaging

claim: Electrical stimulation at 48 hpf for 2 min at 20V caused no visible muscle damage or significant change in tenocyte projection lengths compared to controls.
source: Stimulation at 48 hpf for 2 min at 20V caused no visible muscle damage or significant change in tenocyte projection lengths compared to controls (Figure 2C,E)
evidence: Experimental observation from electrical stimulation protocol

claim: Electrical stimulation of αBtx-injected embryos rescued both tenocyte projection length and density along the VMS almost completely.
source: while the same stimulation of αBtx-injected embryos rescued both tenocyte projection length and density along the VMS almost completely (Figure 2D,E; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Quantitative rescue experiment data

claim: Homozygous cacnb1 mutants paralyzed due to lack of a functional voltage-dependent L-type calcium channel subtype beta-1 showed similar (10–15 μm) reductions in projection length.
source: The observed reductions in projection length and density were caused by paralysis rather than any unanticipated effect of αBtx, since homozygous mutants paralyzed due to lack of a functional voltage-dependent L-type calcium channel subtype beta-1 (Cacnb1), necessary for excitation-contraction coupling in muscle, showed similar (10–15 μm) reductions in projection length (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) (Zhou et al., 2006).
evidence: Genetic mutant analysis with citation for gene function

claim: Tenocytes in cacnb1 mutant embryos fail to compact and elongate.
source: Tenocytes in cacnb1 mutant embryos fail to compact and elongate.
evidence: Morphological observation in genetic mutant

claim: Cranial tenocytes in 4 dpf cacnb1 mutant embryos showed both a failure to compact and elongate, as well as reduced projections and frayed myofibers.
source: We observed both a failure of cranial tenocytes to compact and elongate, as well as reduced projections and frayed myofibers (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Immunostaining observation in mutant embryos

claim: There is a strong correlation between mechanical force from muscle contraction and tenocyte morphogenesis.
source: These results indicate a strong correlation between mechanical force from muscle contraction and tenocyte morphogenesis, suggesting that force stimulates the dynamic growth and branching of tenocyte projections.
evidence: Inference from multiple experimental observations including paralysis and rescue experiments

claim: Tsp4b secreted by tenocytes is essential for ECM organization at MTJs and strengthens muscle attachments.
source: We previously showed that Tsp4b secreted by tenocytes is essential for ECM organization at MTJs and strengthens muscle attachments (Subramanian and Schilling, 2014).
evidence: Citation to previous work by the authors

claim: Injection of tsp4b-gfp full length mRNA into Tg(scxa:mCherry) embryos produced Tsp4b-GFP protein that localized to MTJs along the attachment sites at 48 hpf.
source: Consistent with this, injection of tsp4b-gfp full length mRNA into Tg(scxa:mCherry) embryos produced Tsp4b-GFP protein that localized to MTJs along the attachment sites at 48 hpf (Figure 3A–C,I).
evidence: Experimental observation from mRNA injection and imaging

claim: Exogenous Tsp4b-GFP protein was dramatically reduced in αBtx-injected embryos, particularly around projections, and became diffuse compared to uninjected controls.
source: This exogenous Tsp4b-GFP protein was dramatically reduced in αBtx-injected embryos, particularly around projections, and became diffuse compared to uninjected controls (Figure 3D–F,I).
evidence: Quantitative imaging analysis comparing control and paralyzed embryos

claim: Immunohistochemical staining for Tsp4b at 48 hpf in αBtx-injected embryos showed dramatic reductions along the attachment sites compared to controls.
source: Likewise, immunohistochemical staining for Tsp4b at 48 hpf in αBtx-injected embryos showed dramatic reductions along the attachment sites compared to controls (Figure 3G,H,J).
evidence: Immunostaining quantification data

claim: Laminin at 48 hpf and fibronectin at 24 hpf showed no significant changes at the MTJ in αBtx-injected embryos at 48 hpf.
source: In contrast, other ECM proteins such as laminin (Lam) at 48 hpf and and fibronectin (Fn) at 24 hpf showed no significant changes at the MTJ in αBtx-injected embryos at 48 hpf (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Immunostaining quantification showing no significant difference

claim: Restoring force in paralyzed embryos through electrical stimulation rescued both local levels and the overall area of Tsp4b protein localization along the VMS.
source: Defects in Tsp4b distribution were due to the lack of mechanical force, since restoring force in paralyzed embryos through electrical stimulation rescued both local levels and the overall area of Tsp4b protein localization along the VMS (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Rescue experiment with quantitative imaging analysis

claim: Real-time PCR found a significant reduction in tsp4b expression at 48 hpf in αBtx-injected embryos, while no significant change in expression was observed at 24 hpf.
source: To test the hypothesis that changes in Tsp4b localization were due to reduced tsp4b gene expression in response to lack of force, we performed real-time PCR and found a significant reduction in tsp4b expression at 48 hpf in αBtx-injected embryos, while no significant change in expression was observed at 24 hpf (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: qRT-PCR data showing temporal gene expression changes

claim: Muscle contractions regulate the composition and organization of the tendon ECM.
source: These results suggest a role for mechanical force in both assembly of tendon ECM and expression of key MTJ ECM genes during development and demonstrate that muscle contractions regulate the composition and organization of the tendon ECM.
evidence: Inference from multiple experimental results on ECM protein localization and gene expression

claim: Injection of full-length mRNA encoding eGFP-αtubulin showed that this fusion protein localized to MTs along the length of tenocyte projections.
source: To determine the cytoskeletal structure of tenocyte projections we injected full-length mRNA encoding eGFP-αtubulin and found that this fusion protein localized to MTs along the length of tenocyte projections ﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿ (Figure 4A–C) (Rusan et al., 2001).
evidence: Experimental observation from mRNA injection and live imaging with citation

claim: Similar injections of plasmids encoding EGFP-Lifeact-7 failed to show labeled actin in the tenocyte projections.
source: Similar injections of plasmids encoding EGFP-Lifeact-7 failed to show labeled actin in the projections.
evidence: Negative experimental result from actin labeling

claim: Treatment with Nocodazole caused tenocyte projections to fragment.
source: To determine if MTs are critical for maintaining projections, we treated embryos with Nocodazole, which caused them to fragment (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: Pharmacological perturbation experiment with imaging

claim: Immunohistochemical staining of Nocodazole-treated embryos for Tsp4b showed scattered Tsp4b + puncta localized at MTJs along the VMS and reduced Tsp4b protein levels in the VMS.
source: Immunohistochemical staining of Nocodazole-treated embryos for Tsp4b showed scattered Tsp4b + puncta localized at MTJs along the VMS and reduced Tsp4b protein levels in the VMS (Figure 4F,G,H,I).
evidence: Immunostaining quantification after drug treatment

claim: MTs are the key structural components of tenocyte projections required to sustain the organization of tendon ECM.
source: These results suggest that MTs are the key structural components of tenocyte projections required to sustain the organization of tendon ECM.
evidence: Inference from microtubule labeling and Nocodazole treatment experiments

claim: Treatment with SB431542 (TGFβ receptor inhibitor) for 12 hr from 24 to 36 hpf severely reduced signaling in both muscle fibers and tenocytes as confirmed by immunostaining for phosphorylated SMAD3 (pSMAD3).
source: To address this hypothesis, we treated Tg(scxa:mCherry) embryos with a chemical inhibitor of TGFβ signaling (SB431542 – which blocks TGFβ receptors) for 12 hr from 24 to 36 hpf (Chen and Galloway, 2014). This treatment severely reduced signaling in both muscle fibers and tenocytes as confirmed by immunostaining for phosphorylated SMAD3 (pSMAD3) in SB431542-treated embryos compared to controls (Figure 5A–C,E–G,I).
evidence: Pharmacological inhibition experiment with immunostaining quantification and citation

claim: Tenocyte projections were reduced in length by an average of ~20 μm in SB431542-treated embryos.
source: In addition, tenocyte projections were reduced in length by an average of ~20 μm in SB431542-treated embryos (Figure 5D,H,J), similar to the effects of αBtx (Figure 2B,E).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from imaging after drug treatment

claim: SB431542-treated embryos continued to swim actively despite reduced tenocyte projections.
source: However, unlike embryos injected with αBtx, SB431542-treated embryos continued to swim actively.
evidence: Behavioral observation of drug-treated embryos

claim: TGFβ signaling acts downstream of muscle contraction to stimulate growth and branching of tenocyte projections.
source: These results suggest that TGFβsignaling acts downstream of muscle contraction to stimulate growth and branching of tenocyte projections.
evidence: Inference from TGFβ inhibitor experiments showing projection defects without paralysis

claim: Control embryos showed strong pSMAD3 localization in the nuclei of muscles and tenocytes.
source: To confirm if muscle contraction is essential for activation of TGFβ signaling, we stained control and αBtx-injected, Tg(scx:mCherry) embryos with anti-pSMAD3. While control embryos showed strong pSMAD3 localization in the nuclei of muscles and tenocytes, pSMAD3 staining was strongly reduced in the nuclei of tenocytes in αBtx-injected embryos (Figure 6A–G).
evidence: Immunostaining observation in control embryos

claim: pSMAD3 staining was strongly reduced in the nuclei of tenocytes in αBtx-injected embryos.
source: While control embryos showed strong pSMAD3 localization in the nuclei of muscles and tenocytes, pSMAD3 staining was strongly reduced in the nuclei of tenocytes in αBtx-injected embryos (Figure 6A–G).
evidence: Immunostaining quantification in paralyzed embryos

claim: In αBtx-injected embryos, paralysis specifically reduced pSMAD3 in tenocytes and not in muscle nuclei, in contrast to embryos treated with SB431542.
source: Here, in contrast to embryos treated with SB431542 (Figure 5C,G), paralysis specifically reduced pSMAD3 in tenocytes and not in muscle nuclei.
evidence: Comparative immunostaining analysis between different experimental conditions

claim: Reduction in pSMAD3 in paralyzed embryos correlated with the reduction in length of tenocyte projections.
source: This correlated with the reduction in length of tenocyte projections (Figure 6H).
evidence: Correlation analysis between signaling and morphology measurements

claim: Mechanical force from muscle contraction serves as a cue for TGFβ mediated signaling in tenocytes to control their morphogenesis and differentiation.
source: These results suggest that mechanical force from muscle contraction serves as a cue for TGFβ mediated signaling in tenocytes to control their morphogenesis and differentiation.
evidence: Inference from experiments showing force-dependent pSMAD3 activation and projection changes

claim: αBtx-injected embryos stimulated with mild electric current showed increased pSMAD3 localization in tenocyte nuclei.
source: To further confirm that mechanical force has a role in induction of TGF-β responses in tenocytes, we stained control and αBtx-injected embryos with or without electrical stimulation, with anti-pSMAD3 antibody to verify if localization of pSMAD3 in nuclei of tenocytes could be rescued. αBtx-injected embryos stimulated with mild electric current showed increased pSMAD3 localization in tenocyte nuclei strongly suggesting that mechanical force from muscle contraction can rescue TGFβ signaling in tenocytes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Rescue experiment with immunostaining quantification

claim: Real-time PCR analysis on cDNA prepared from 48 hpf control and αBtx-injected embryos revealed that paralysis led to an almost complete loss of expression of tsp4b, tgfbip, and ctgfa, while expression levels of scxa were unaffected.
source: Real-time PCR analysis on cDNA prepared from 48 hpf control and αBtx-injected embryos revealed that paralysis led to an almost complete loss of expression of tsp4b, as well as TGFβ-induced protein (tgfbip) and, connective tissue growth factor a (ctgfa), while expression levels of other tendon genes, such as scxa, were unaffected (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: qRT-PCR data showing differential gene expression changes

claim: All three genes (tsp4b, tgfbip and ctgfa) were restored to control levels of expression with electrical stimulation.
source: All three genes (tsp4b, tgfbip and ctgfa) were restored to control levels of expression with electrical stimulation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: qRT-PCR data from rescue experiments

claim: ddPCR results from whole embryo cDNA preparation agreed with the real-time PCR analysis.
source: We further validated the results with digital droplet PCR (ddPCR) on cDNA prepared from FACS sorted tenocytes and whole embryos respectively. Our ddPCR results from whole embryo cDNA preparation agreed with the real-time PCR analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: ddPCR validation data

claim: Real-time PCR analysis of SB431542-treated embryos showed significant reductions in expression of tsp4b and tgfbip genes.
source: Real-time PCR analysis of SB431542-treated embryos showed significant reductions in expression of tsp4b and tgfbip genes (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: qRT-PCR data from TGFβ inhibitor treatment

claim: Loss of tenocyte projections through destabilization of microtubules in nocodazole-treated embryos led to reduced expression of tsp4b and tgfbip while expression of ctgfa and scxa were elevated.
source: Loss of tenocyte projections through destabilization of microtubules in nocodazole-treated embryos also led to reduced expression of tsp4b and tgfbip while expression of ctgfa and scxa were elevated (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: qRT-PCR data from Nocodazole treatment

claim: Mechanical force acts through TGFβ signaling to regulate tenocyte-specific transcription including ECM components such as Tsp4b.
source: Taken together, these results are consistent with the hypothesis that mechanical force acts through TGFβ signaling to regulate tenocyte-specific transcription including ECM components such as Tsp4b.
evidence: Inference from multiple gene expression experiments under different conditions

claim: Early developing tenocytes in zebrafish express the tenogenic fate determinant, scxa, prior to the differentiation of muscle fibers.
source: Here we show that early developing tenocytes in zebrafish express the tenogenic fate determinant, scxa, prior to the differentiation of muscle fibers and respond to the onset of muscle contraction by elongating and extending an array of polarized projections.
evidence: Summary of experimental observations from transgenic line analysis

claim: Tenocytes respond to the onset of muscle contraction by elongating and extending an array of polarized projections.
source: Here we show that early developing tenocytes in zebrafish express the tenogenic fate determinant, scxa, prior to the differentiation of muscle fibers and respond to the onset of muscle contraction by elongating and extending an array of polarized projections.
evidence: Summary of morphological observations correlated with muscle contraction

claim: Tenocyte projections are disrupted by changes in force as is the corresponding organization of the tendon ECM, which is critical for MTJ function.
source: These projections are disrupted by changes in force as is the corresponding organization of the tendon ECM, which is critical for MTJ function (Subramanian and Schilling, 2014).
evidence: Summary of experimental results with citation to previous work

claim: TGFβ signaling responses induced by mechanical force from muscle contraction correlate with changes in tenocyte morphogenesis and tendon ECM composition during tendon development.
source: Our results show for the first time in vivo that TGFβ signaling responses induced by mechanical force from muscle contraction correlate with changes in tenocyte morphogenesis and tendon ECM composition during tendon development.
evidence: Summary of novel findings from multiple experiments

claim: Tenocyte projections function as force sensors and responders in the feedback between tenocyte and ECM that physically balance responses to mechanical force.
source: These results suggest a novel role for tenocyte projections as force sensors and responders in the feedback between tenocyte and ECM that physically balance responses to mechanical force (Figure 7).
evidence: Inference from all experimental data synthesized into a model

claim: Tendons primarily experience tension from muscle contractions.
source: Tendons primarily experience tension from muscle contractions (Lavagnino et al., 2015; Wang, 2006).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to literature

claim: Skeletal cell types (e.g. osteocytes, osteoblasts, chondrocytes) are exposed to compressive forces.
source: In contrast, skeletal cell types (e.g. osteocytes, osteoblasts, chondrocytes) are exposed to compressive forces (Klein-Nulend et al., 2012)
evidence: Statement supported by citation to literature

claim: Chondrocytes in joints are exposed to shear forces from fluid flow.
source: or shear forces in the case of chondrocytes in joints exposed to fluid flow (Servin-Vences et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to literature

claim: In the absence of tension during development, tenocytes reduce the extent and spread of their projections into the tendon ECM and this can be rescued by a short bout of contraction.
source: We show that in the absence of tension during development, tenocytes reduce the extent and spread of their projections into the tendon ECM and this can be rescued by a short bout of contraction.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from paralysis and rescue experiments

claim: Tendon defects and injuries result from dramatic changes in tension experienced either instantly or periodically over extended periods of muscle disuse or overuse.
source: Tendon defects and injuries result from dramatic changes in tension experienced either instantly or periodically over extended periods of muscle disuse or overuse (Franchi et al., 2013; Gaut and Duprez, 2016; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to literature

claim: The establishment and adaptation of MTJs occurs in response to mechanical force from muscle contraction and involves both changes in tenocyte morphogenesis and ECM production.
source: Our results support the idea that the establishment and adaptation of MTJs occurs in response to mechanical force from muscle contraction and involves both changes in tenocyte morphogenesis and ECM production.
evidence: Inference from experimental results

claim: Early experiments on developing chick embryos have shown that induced lack of muscle activity negatively affects the growth of associated skeletal structures.
source: Early experiments on developing chick embryos have shown that induced lack of muscle activity (either by lack of neuronal innervation or by injecting paralysis-inducing drugs) negatively affects the growth of associated skeletal structures, suggesting a role for force from muscle contraction as an essential cue for proper growth and differentiation of the skeleton (Hall and Herring, 1990; Hamburger and Waugh, 1940).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to historical literature

claim: During development, the skeleton is exposed to two major types of force – contractile (tension) force from muscles and compressional force (e.g. gravity).
source: During development, the skeleton is exposed to two major types of force – contractile (tension) force from muscles and compressional force (e.g. gravity).
evidence: General knowledge about skeletal biomechanics

claim: A contractile force from muscles has a greater impact on the growth of bones when compared to compression.
source: A contractile force from muscles has a greater impact on the growth of bones when compared to compression, indicating a primary role for muscle function in guiding the growth of associated skeletal tissues (Ellman et al., 2014; Warden et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to literature

claim: Recent studies in paralyzed limbs have shown that the development of a tendon-bone attachment unit, the enthesis, is affected by lack of muscle contraction.
source: Recent studies in paralyzed limbs have shown that the development of a tendon-bone attachment unit, the enthesis, is affected by lack of muscle contraction (Schwartz et al., 2013; Tatara et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to literature

claim: Muscle contraction has a role in the development of tendons.
source: Our studies suggest that muscle contraction has a similar role in the development of tendons.
evidence: Inference from current study results compared to literature

claim: Immobilization experiments performed on canine models have shown that mechanical force is required for repair of tendon injuries.
source: Immobilization experiments performed on canine models have shown that mechanical force is required for repair of tendon injuries (Gelberman et al., 1982).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to literature

claim: Recent studies using paralysis and restricted movement have shown that mechanical force has multiple roles in the maintenance of tenogenic gene expression, secretion of tendon ECM, and tenocyte survival.
source: More recent studies using paralysis and restricted movement have shown that mechanical force has multiple roles in the maintenance of tenogenic gene expression, secretion of tendon ECM, and tenocyte survival (Gaut et al., 2016; Hettrich et al., 2011; Maeda et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to literature

claim: Tenocyte projections have been reported in electron micrographs of mammalian tendon fascicles.
source: Tenocyte projections have been reported in electron micrographs of mammalian tendon fascicles yet how they form and their functions in tendon development remain largely unexplored (Kalson et al., 2015; Knudsen et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to literature

claim: Tenocytes play an active role in sensing force and thereby regulating ECM composition and overall tendon strength.
source: Our results suggest that tenocytes play an active role in sensing force and thereby regulating ECM composition and overall tendon strength.
evidence: Inference from experimental results

claim: The force of muscle contraction regulates the growth and branching of tenocyte projections via TGFβ signaling.
source: In addition, we show that the force of muscle contraction regulates the growth and branching of tenocyte projections via TGFβ signaling.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: Feedback between tenocytes and ECM may be a common mechanism for force adaptation within the musculoskeletal system.
source: Such feedback between tenocytes and ECM may be a common mechanism for force adaptation within the musculoskeletal system.
evidence: Speculation based on current findings

claim: Tenocytes in Drosophila rely on a network of polarized MTs for the maintenance of cellular structure and function.
source: Tenocytes in Drosophila rely on a network of polarized MTs for the maintenance of cellular structure and function (Subramanian et al., 2003), but similar requirements for cytoskeletal components have not been investigated in vertebrate tendons.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to literature

claim: Zebrafish tenocytes are rich in MTs, which are required to maintain projections.
source: Here, we show that zebrafish tenocytes are rich in MTs, which are required to maintain projections.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from tubulin labeling and Nocodazole experiments

claim: Pharmacological disruption of MTs destabilized the tenocyte projections without affecting tenocyte cell bodies.
source: Pharmacological disruption of MTs destabilized the projections without affecting tenocyte cell bodies.
evidence: Observation from Nocodazole treatment experiments

claim: Tenocyte projections both sense force and respond to it by altering ECM organization in an MT-dependent manner.
source: This reduced Tsp4b localization suggesting that tenocyte projections both sense force and respond to it by altering ECM organization in an MT-dependent manner.
evidence: Inference from Nocodazole experiments showing reduced Tsp4b

claim: Treatment of embryos with Nocodazole causes global destabilization of MT in the entire embryo.
source: A caveat to this result is that treatment of embryos with Nocodazole causes global destabilization of MT in the entire embryo.
evidence: Acknowledgment of experimental limitation

claim: The effects on tenocyte projections and tendon ECM organization from Nocodazole could arise in response to MT destabilization in neighboring muscle fibers, axons and other cells.
source: Hence, the effects on tenocyte projections and tendon ECM organization could also arise in response to MT destabilization in neighboring muscle fibers, axons and other cells.
evidence: Speculation about alternative explanations for experimental results

claim: Airinemes in pigment cells are composed of both F-actin and MTs and play a role in long-range signaling by secreting signaling ligands at the tips of their projections.
source: Similar roles for cellular projections have been observed in pigment cells, where airinemes composed of both F-actin and MTs play a role in long-range signaling by secreting signaling ligands at the tips of their projections (Eom et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to literature

claim: Loss of tenocyte projections leads to upregulated expression of scxa and ctgfa in MT-deficient embryos, suggesting that they revert to a more dedifferentiated state.
source: We find that loss of tenocyte projections leads to upregulated expression of scxa and ctgfa in MT-deficient embryos, suggesting that they revert to a more dedifferentiated state.
evidence: Inference from gene expression data in Nocodazole-treated embryos

claim: Previous EM studies of human and rat tendons have described tenocytes projecting into the tendon matrix, but their functional significance has remained unclear.
source: Previous EM studies of human and rat tendons have described tenocytes projecting into the tendon matrix, but their functional significance has remained unclear (McNeilly et al., 1996; Pingel et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to literature

claim: 3D reconstructions from EM studies suggest a role for tenocyte projections, referred to as 'fibropositors' in one study, in secreting collagen fibrils.
source: 3D reconstructions from EM studies suggest a role for these projections, referred to as 'fibropositors' in one study, in secreting collagen fibrils (Canty et al., 2004).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to literature

claim: Analysis of Scx expression in chick and mouse using immunostaining and transgenic reporter lines have shown that limb tendons elongate as the musculoskeletal system matures.
source: Analysis of Scx expression in chick and mouse using immunostaining and transgenic reporter lines, respectively, have shown that limb tendons elongate as the musculoskeletal system matures (Brent et al., 2003; Kardon, 1998; Pryce et al., 2007).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to literature

claim: Elongated tenocyte projections are conserved across species, but are quite distinct in different classes of tenocytes.
source: Our results in zebrafish reveal that such elongated projections are conserved, but quite distinct in different classes of tenocytes.
evidence: Inference from comparative observations in zebrafish

claim: Cranial tenocytes resemble limb tenocytes in that they extend in parallel to the direction of force.
source: While cranial tenocytes resemble those in the limb in that they extend in parallel to the direction of force, axial tenocytes extend their projections perpendicular to the plane of muscle contraction (with opposing directions of contractile force) (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Comparative morphological observation from imaging

claim: Axial tenocytes extend their projections perpendicular to the plane of muscle contraction.
source: While cranial tenocytes resemble those in the limb in that they extend in parallel to the direction of force, axial tenocytes extend their projections perpendicular to the plane of muscle contraction (with opposing directions of contractile force) (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Morphological observation from imaging

claim: Distinct tenocyte morphologies reflect a more structural, load-bearing role for cranial (and limb) tenocytes, while early larval axial tenocytes in zebrafish function as tension sensors in the myoseptum.
source: Based on our results, we propose that these distinct morphologies reflect a more structural, load-bearing role for cranial (and limb) tenocytes, while early larval axial tenocytes in zebrafish function as tension sensors in the myoseptum.
evidence: Hypothesis proposed based on morphological observations

claim: The timing of the outgrowth of tenocyte projections tightly correlates with the onset of muscle contraction.
source: Consistent with the tension-sensor hypothesis, the timing of the outgrowth of tenocyte projections tightly correlates with the onset of muscle contraction.
evidence: Temporal correlation observed from developmental time course

claim: Osteocytes extend projections into the bone matrix where they are thought to form a network of force sensors.
source: Tension sensing projections are observed in other musculoskeletal tissues as osteocytes extend projections into the bone matrix where they are thought to form a network of force sensors (Cowin et al., 1991) that modulate bone formation and resorption (Klein-Nulend et al., 2012; Schaffler et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to literature

claim: Osteocyte projections modulate bone formation and resorption.
source: Tension sensing projections are observed in other musculoskeletal tissues as osteocytes extend projections into the bone matrix where they are thought to form a network of force sensors (Cowin et al., 1991) that modulate bone formation and resorption (Klein-Nulend et al., 2012; Schaffler et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to literature

claim: The cues that cause osteoblasts to form projections as they differentiate into osteocytes remain unknown.
source: Likewise, the cues that cause osteoblasts to form these projections as they differentiate into osteocytes remain unknown (Franz-Odendaal et al., 2006).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to literature

claim: Mammalian osteocyte projections increase in density in response to force, consistent with a role as force sensors and responders.
source: Similar to our results with zebrafish tenocytes, mammalian osteocyte projections increase in density in response to force, consistent with a role as force sensors and responders in both cases.
evidence: Comparison to literature on osteocytes

claim: In both bone and tendon, the ECM undergoes dynamic changes in expression of collagens, fibronectin, laminin and MMPs.
source: In both bone and tendon, the ECM undergoes dynamic changes in expression of collagens, fibronectin, laminin and MMPs, and this is also the case in the developing somites of zebrafish embryos (Jenkins et al., 2016; Snow and Henry, 2009).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to literature

claim: Tenocyte projection formation correlates with the establishment of tendon ECM.
source: Tenocyte projection formation also correlates with the establishment of tendon ECM.
evidence: Temporal correlation observed in current study

claim: Previous studies have shown remodeling of MTJ ECM between 24 and 48 hpf with a progressive reduction of Fn, which is replaced by increased levels of Lam at the MTJ.
source: Previous studies have shown remodeling of MTJ ECM between 24 and 48 hpf with a progressive reduction of Fn, which is replaced by increased in levels of Lam at the MTJ (Jenkins et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to literature

claim: Initial production and accumulation of Fn is independent of force at 24 hpf, when tsp4b also shows force-independent expression.
source: Our results suggest that initial production and accumulation of Fn is independent of force at 24 hpf, when tsp4b also shows force-independent expression.
evidence: Inference from gene expression and protein localization data at 24 hpf

claim: The later force-dependent expression and localization of Tsp4b at 48 hpf indicates that dynamic regulation of tendon ECM occurs after the onset of muscle contraction.
source: The later force-dependent expression and localization of Tsp4b at 48 hpf indicates that dynamic regulation of tendon ECM occurs after the onset of muscle contraction, which suggests a role for mechanical force in the process.
evidence: Inference from temporal gene expression and protein localization data

claim: Mammalian tenocytes actively sense mechanical force in vitro, resulting in changes in gene expression, cytoskeletal organization and ECM secretion.
source: Mammalian tenocytes actively sense mechanical force in vitro, resulting in changes in gene expression, cytoskeletal organization and ECM secretion (Banos et al., 2008; Gaut et al., 2016; Havis et al., 2016; Maeda et al., 2010; Maeda et al., 2013; Maeda et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to literature

claim: Mechanosensing in mammalian tenocytes depends, at least in part, on gap junctional complexes that localize to tenocyte projections.
source: This depends, at least in part, on gap junctional complexes that localize to tenocyte projections (Maeda et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to literature

claim: Exercise induces Tenomodulin (Tnmd) and Col1a1 expression and tenocyte proliferation in rats.
source: Exercise induces Tenomodulin (Tnmd) and Col1a1 expression and tenocyte proliferation in rats (Eliasson et al., 2009; Zhang and Wang, 2013)
evidence: Statement supported by citations to literature

claim: Stress induces COL4A1 and COL6A1 expression in chick tenocytes.
source: and stress induces COL4A1 and COL6A1 expression in chick tenocytes (Marturano et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to literature

claim: The molecular mechanisms underlying cellular signaling responses to force in tenocytes are unclear.
source: Despite these changes in gene expression, the molecular mechanisms underlying these cellular signaling responses to force are unclear.
evidence: Statement about knowledge gap in the field

claim: Embryonic tenocyte projections in zebrafish end in bouton-like structures close to the dermis, which may act as signaling beacons and ECM secreting centers.
source: Embryonic tenocyte projections in zebrafish end in bouton-like structures close to the dermis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B), which may act as signaling beacons and ECM secreting centers.
evidence: Morphological observation with speculation about function

claim: The strong correlation between onset of muscle function, changing myotendinous ECM and tenocyte morphogenesis suggests a model in which force is transduced through cues from the ECM that induce the formation of projections.
source: The strong correlation between onset of muscle function, changing myotendinous ECM and tenocyte morphogenesis suggests a model in which force is transduced through cues from the ECM that induce the formation of projections (Figure 7A).
evidence: Model proposed based on correlations observed in the study

claim: Similar processes may underlie the projections of osteocytes and other mesenchymal cell types.
source: Similar processes may underlie the projections of osteocytes and other mesenchymal cell types.
evidence: Speculation about broader applicability of findings

claim: Feedback between tenocytes and ECM likely allows tendons to adapt to changing mechanical force during normal development and exercise, as well as in healing and repair of tendon injuries.
source: Such feedback likely allows tendons to adapt to changing mechanical force during normal development and exercise, as well as in healing and repair of tendon injuries.
evidence: Speculation about functional significance of findings

claim: Mechanical forces between cells and extracellular matrix (ECM) influence cell shape and function.
source: Mechanical forces between cells and extracellular matrix (ECM) influence cell shape and function.
evidence: General statement of established knowledge in the field

claim: Tendons are ECM-rich tissues connecting muscles with bones that bear extreme tensional force.
source: Tendons are ECM-rich tissues connecting muscles with bones that bear extreme tensional force.
evidence: General anatomical and functional knowledge

claim: Tenocyte fibroblasts extend arrays of microtubule-rich projections at the onset of muscle contraction.
source: Analysis of transgenic zebrafish expressing mCherry driven by the tendon determinant scleraxis reveals that tendon fibroblasts (tenocytes) extend arrays of microtubule-rich projections at the onset of muscle contraction.
evidence: Summary of key finding from the study

claim: In the trunk, tenocyte projections form a dense curtain along the myotendinous junctions at somite boundaries, perpendicular to myofibers.
source: In the trunk, these form a dense curtain along the myotendinous junctions at somite boundaries, perpendicular to myofibers, suggesting a role as force sensors to control ECM production and tendon strength.
evidence: Morphological observation from imaging

claim: Tenocyte projections may function as force sensors to control ECM production and tendon strength.
source: In the trunk, these form a dense curtain along the myotendinous junctions at somite boundaries, perpendicular to myofibers, suggesting a role as force sensors to control ECM production and tendon strength.
evidence: Hypothesis based on morphological observations

claim: Paralysis or destabilization of microtubules reduces tenocyte projection length and surrounding ECM.
source: Paralysis or destabilization of microtubules reduces projection length and surrounding ECM, both of which are rescued by muscle stimulation.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: Both projection length and surrounding ECM are rescued by muscle stimulation.
source: Paralysis or destabilization of microtubules reduces projection length and surrounding ECM, both of which are rescued by muscle stimulation.
evidence: Summary of rescue experiment results

claim: Paralysis reduces SMAD3 phosphorylation in tenocytes.
source: Paralysis also reduces SMAD3 phosphorylation in tenocytes and chemical inhibition of TGFβ signaling shortens tenocyte projections.
evidence: Summary of signaling analysis results

claim: Chemical inhibition of TGFβ signaling shortens tenocyte projections.
source: Paralysis also reduces SMAD3 phosphorylation in tenocytes and chemical inhibition of TGFβ signaling shortens tenocyte projections.
evidence: Summary of pharmacological inhibition results

claim: TGFβ, released in response to force, acts on tenocytes to alter their morphology and ECM production.
source: These results suggest that TGFβ, released in response to force, acts on tenocytes to alter their morphology and ECM production, revealing a feedback mechanism by which tendons adapt to tension.
evidence: Model proposed based on experimental results

claim: There is a feedback mechanism by which tendons adapt to tension.
source: These results suggest that TGFβ, released in response to force, acts on tenocytes to alter their morphology and ECM production, revealing a feedback mechanism by which tendons adapt to tension.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental results
